title: Kubernetes Core Workloads: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of cluster architecture, Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, rolling updates and rollbacks, and the kubectl commands you use daily. It ends with common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: What This Handbook Covers
points: Cluster architecture
Pods
ReplicaSets and Deployments
Rolling updates and rollbacks
kubectl essentials and cheat sheet

chapters.title: Cluster Architecture: Control Plane and Nodes
points: Control plane components: kube-apiserver (the only front door; all components talk through it), etcd (key-value store holding all cluster state), kube-scheduler (picks a node for unassigned Pods), kube-controller-manager (runs control loops that move actual state toward desired state)
Node components: kubelet (makes sure the containers in assigned Pods are running), kube-proxy (programs Service routing rules), container runtime (containerd or CRI-O runs the containers)
Declarative loop: you submit desired state to the API server, it is stored in etcd, controllers watch for drift and fix it, the scheduler binds a Pod to a node, and the kubelet starts it

Control plane vs worker node: the control plane decides and stores, workers run the application Pods. Only the API server reads and writes etcd, and the kubelet reports node and Pod status back to the API server
Gotcha: losing etcd without a backup loses the whole cluster's state, while running Pods keep running until the node fails. Check with `kubectl get nodes` and `kubectl get pods -n kube-system`

chapters.title: Pods: The Smallest Deployable Unit
points: A Pod wraps one or more containers that share one network namespace (a single Pod IP, containers reach each other on localhost) and can share volumes. Multi-container Pods are for tightly coupled helpers such as sidecars
Pod lifecycle phases: Pending (waiting to be scheduled or pulling images), Running, Succeeded, Failed. Containers are restarted according to restartPolicy (Always, OnFailure, Never)
Pod vs container: you schedule Pods, not containers, and a Pod is ephemeral. A replaced Pod gets a new name and a new IP, so never depend on a Pod IP

Minimal manifest: `apiVersion: v1`, `kind: Pod`, `metadata.name`, and `spec.containers` with `name`, `image` and `ports.containerPort`. Run it with `kubectl apply -f pod.yaml`, or quickly with `kubectl run web --image=nginx`

Common mistakes: running bare Pods in production (nothing recreates them if the node dies), setting no resource requests or limits, and using the `latest` tag. The usual failure states are ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff and Pending, and `kubectl describe pod` shows the Events that explain them

chapters.title: ReplicaSets and Deployments
points: A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods running. It matches Pods by `selector.matchLabels` and creates or deletes Pods to equal `spec.replicas`

A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds updates and rollback. The chain is Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Each change to the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet and keeps the old ones for rollback

Deployment vs ReplicaSet vs bare Pod: a bare Pod has no self-healing, a ReplicaSet gives self-healing and scaling but no update strategy, and a Deployment gives all of that plus rolling updates and history. Use Deployments for stateless apps

Deployment manifest: `apiVersion: apps/v1`, `kind: Deployment`, `metadata.name: web`, `spec.replicas: 3`, `selector.matchLabels: {app: web}`, and `template.metadata.labels: {app: web}` followed by `template.spec.containers`. Create one with `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3`

Gotcha: `selector.matchLabels` must match `template.metadata.labels`, or the API rejects the Deployment. The selector is immutable after creation. Scale with `kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5`, and change replicas in Git rather than hand-editing a live object

chapters.title: Rolling Updates, Rollbacks and kubectl Essentials
points: Rolling update (the default strategy): the new ReplicaSet scales up while the old one scales down, so the app stays available. `maxSurge` (extra Pods allowed, default 25%) and `maxUnavailable` (Pods allowed down, default 25%) control the pace

Rolling update vs Recreate: RollingUpdate gives zero downtime but both versions run side by side during the update. Recreate kills all old Pods first, so there is downtime, and it suits apps that cannot run two versions at once

Update and watch: `kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.27` or edit the YAML and `kubectl apply -f`, then `kubectl rollout status deploy/web`. Only a change to the Pod template triggers a rollout, and scaling does not

Rollback: `kubectl rollout history deploy/web` lists revisions, `kubectl rollout undo deploy/web` returns to the previous one, and `--to-revision=2` picks a specific one. `kubectl rollout pause` and `resume` hold a rollout while you batch changes. `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10) caps how many old ReplicaSets are kept

Mistakes: no readiness probe, so traffic reaches Pods that are not ready and a bad image still looks like a successful rollout. Also forgetting `-n <namespace>` (you query the wrong namespace) and debugging in the wrong order. Debug in this order: `kubectl get`, `describe`, `logs` (add `--previous` after a crash), then `exec -it <pod> -- sh`

chapters.title: Kubernetes Core Cheat Sheet
points: Architecture: control plane = apiserver + etcd + scheduler + controller-manager. Node = kubelet + kube-proxy + container runtime. Chain: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod

Inspect: `kubectl get pods -o wide`, `kubectl describe pod

`, `kubectl logs

-f`, `kubectl exec -it

-- sh`, `kubectl get all -n `

Create and change: `kubectl apply -f file.yaml`, `kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx`, `kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5`, `kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.27`, `kubectl delete -f file.yaml`
Rollout: `kubectl rollout status|history|undo|pause|resume deploy/web`, with `--to-revision=N` to pick a revision. Defaults: maxSurge 25%, maxUnavailable 25%, revisionHistoryLimit 10

Troubleshooting map: Pending = no node fits or the scheduler has not placed it. ImagePullBackOff = wrong image or registry credentials. CrashLoopBackOff = the app keeps crashing, so read `logs --previous`. Add `-n <ns>` or `-A` to every query, and `kubectl explain <resource>.spec` shows the field docs
